title: Isoka, Angel of Serpents
subtitle: The Skin Left on the Road

lore.description:
Isoka, sister to Ikasha (Shadow) and Inaea (Mercy), completes the Triad of Transformation. Where thresholds and compassion mark her sisters' domains, Isoka teaches that every self is temporary — identity is a skin to be shed so growth can continue. Her serpents are omens and teachers: each cast skin a lesson in release; each venom a catalyst for necessary change. Those who walk her path become alchemists of the self, embracing dissolution as the first motion of rebirth.

**The Copperhead under an old name.**

Acasian Copperhead houses preserve the names of former selves in ways they will not explain to their clients. A court may hire a new servant without knowing that a related household once sheltered the same person under another face. Those channels began as routes away from inherited obligations and have also become useful to people who want to enter a rival's household unrecognized.

The keepers dispute what must survive a change. One insists that a promise deliberately made should still bind the person who remembers making it. Another regards any enduring claim as a piece of skin that has not been shed. Their disagreement has become more dangerous as clients began purchasing a new life without leaving the possessions gained in the old one.

**The Tide-Shedder at Zakov.**

At the sunken temple, Zakov's devotees leave a lock of hair and a name for the eels. Returning sailors brought versions of the observance into dock neighborhoods, where a basin sometimes stands in for water they cannot reach. The basin is a devotional object, not an automatic substitute for any rite's required place or materials.

A household can celebrate a relative escaping a former identity and still need to know whether that relative intends to return. Some keepers insist on a farewell before the shedding. Others shelter people for whom a farewell would alert a pursuer. The cult's quarrels cannot be resolved by declaring every old tie either sacred or abusive.

**River serpents and forms that are not hers.**

In Dhaharan river towns, some shrine interpreters identify Isoka with the Lady of the Loosened Coil, approached when a household must change its place or standing. Neighboring keepers reject the identification and maintain that their local serpent guardian protects continuity rather than dissolution. They may share an offering place and refuse to share an initiation.

Ayokhan river Vigils have similarly learned to ask what a visiting serpent image means before treating it as evidence of an Isokan rite. A local water presence does not become Isoka because both are pictured with scales. Nor does every Lethai-ar who has shed an old identity belong to her cult. The Woven and the Shed have their own oaths and natures. An observer's convenient classification does not replace them.

**What the Scale-Mothers keep.**

Valewood Scale-Mothers attend changes whose consequences are visible before their meaning can be agreed. Their care may be patient and frightening at once. A devotee can seek release from an intolerable life without deserving every transformation a cult leader is willing to call progress. Keep the chthonic danger: an initiated person may return with habits, appetites, or absences that their loved ones cannot regard as recovery.

Theona has no snakes. Do not supply it with a hidden Isokan serpent sanctuary to complete a map, or use a foreign priest to explain the absence. A returning devotee who cannot reproduce an observance there has encountered a limit, not an invitation to reveal the setting's secret.

For play, a former initiate asks for help keeping a promise their new teacher says no longer belongs to them. The question is what remains theirs to choose, with real people depending on the answer.
lore.followers: Her followers range from quiet hedgewitches who use venom to heal and shed skins to ease grief, to the darker cults of the Coiled Heart, where initiates drink serpent venom to burn away their old selves and emerge as something new — or something monstrous. Isoka does not judge; she offers the knife and the poison both. The choice is the seeker's. Among the peoples of Fate's Edge, Isoka is called by many names. In Zakov, she is the Tide-Shedder, to whom pirates leave a lock of hair and a name at her sunken temple; eels eat both. In Acasia, she is the Copperhead, a hedge-cult that sheds identities to infiltrate noble houses. In the Valewood, her witches are called Scale-Mothers, who tend the boundary between the living and the shedding dead. Wherever change is feared or embraced, Isoka watches.
lore.quote: Do not mourn the skin you shed. It was never meant to last. The venom that burns away the old self is the same that grants the strength to become new.

domain_focus: Serpentine Transformation: shedding identity, renewal through dissolution
Venom as Catalyst: poison that heals or destroys, the paradox of change
Shedding the Past: erasing debts, memories, and old allegiances
Healthy Change to Monstrous Rebirth: from gentle alchemy to sword-and-sorcery cults

thiasos.description: Isoka's Thiasos is a small creature of shedding and renewal: a snake that sheds its skin weekly, a gecko that regrows its tail, a salamander that thrives in the ashes of a burned identity, a small adder that sheds its venom with each bite, or a blind worm that lives beneath the earth and emerges only to transform.
thiasos.care: Beyond its ordinary care, this Thiasos must be allowed to shed something (skin, a tooth, a claw) each week. If that need goes unmet, the Thiasos becomes Compromised: it grows dull and sluggish, and its keeper suffers –1 die on rolls to resist unwanted transformation or change until it next sheds.

codex.description: Isoka's Codex is never a book of fixed ink. It may be a bundle of shed snakeskins, each inscribed with a single Rite that fades as the skin dries; a slate that must be washed clean after each reading; a scroll of living parchment that flakes away as the Rite is learned; or a set of obsidian tablets that must be shattered and recarved after each use.
codex.upkeep: Because Isoka's truths are written in the act of shedding, the Codex requires upkeep: the Runekeeper must spend an hour each week re-inscribing the Rites from memory onto fresh material (new skin, new slate), or the patterns become illegible (treat as Compromised until re-inscribed).

patrons_gift.name: Isoka's Blessing
patrons_gift.description: Once per scene as an action, a Runekeeper of Isoka may touch a held item (weapon, tool, or garment) and whisper a word of shedding.
patrons_gift.effect: For the rest of the scene, the item grants +1 die to Escape or Deception rolls, and the first time each scene the bearer would be bound, grappled, or restrained, they may break free as a free action (shedding the constraint like a snake sheds its skin).
patrons_gift.cost: After the scene, the user marks +1 Obligation to Isoka.

rites.name: Rite of the Loosening Skin
rites.materials: A discarded snakeskin or a strand of your own hair.
rites.effect: Shrug off a temporary burden. Remove one Condition (Fear, Poison, Fatigue, or a minor social stain) that you have acquired this scene. Alternatively, reroll one failed roll to escape restraint or pursuit.
rites.push_it: Also ignore one environmental penalty (difficult terrain, smoke, etc.) for the scene, but leave a visible trace of your passage. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Forked Tongue
rites.materials: A harmless lie whispered to a mirror.
rites.effect: For one scene, you may speak ambiguously without penalty. When you use Deception or Sway to conceal your true intent or pass as someone else, you may treat a Partial Success as a Clean Success (the lie holds). On a Miss, however, the GM gains 2 SB as your deceit unravels in an embarrassing way.
rites.push_it: Extend the effect to one willing ally; they may also lie freely for the scene. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Shedded Self
rites.materials: A complete change of clothing and a token from your former role (a badge, a lock of hair, a written name).
rites.effect: You shed one persistent identity — a title, a bond, a debt, or a reputation. For the remainder of the scene, you are treated as a stranger to those who knew you in that role. You gain +2 dice on any roll to avoid detection, escape pursuit, or convince others that you are not yourself. Create a 6-segment Shed Identity timer; when it fills, the old identity returns as a separate NPC (a rival, a witness, or a ghost).
rites.push_it: Immediately erase one minor obligation (a Debt Timer segment or 1 Obligation to a Patron) as you slough it off. Mark 1 SB (Clubs) as the discarded debt finds a new debtor. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of Venom's Paradox
rites.materials: A drop of venom from a serpent that has shed its skin within the last day.
rites.effect: Inflict or cure through poison's paradox. Choose one: Cursed Venom: Touch a creature and inject venom. They suffer +1 Harm (poison) and must test Resolve (DV 4) or gain the Poisoned Condition (–1 die to physical actions until cured). Mercy's Antidote: Touch a poisoned or diseased creature. The venom neutralizes the malady; remove one Poisoned or Diseased Condition, and the target clears 1 Fatigue.
rites.push_it: Apply both effects to the same target (curse and cleanse in a painful purge, representing a violent rebirth), or affect two different targets. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of Unremembered Metamorphosis
rites.materials: A full identity kit, a serpent's shed skin, and a personal item from the life you are leaving (or records of your old life to burn).
rites.effect: Choose one: Complete Metamorphosis: After an hour of ritual, you emerge with a new face, voice, and documented identity. For one week, you are immune to recognition by anyone who knew your previous self, and gain +2 dice on all Deception and Stealth rolls related to that new identity. Create an 8-segment New Identity timer; when it fills, the old self may reassert itself (GM's discretion). Cast-Off History: After a full night's ritual burning all mundane records of your old life, your previous identity becomes unreliable. Common records and casual memories become vague; those who track you via that identity suffer –2 dice. You gain +2 dice on rolls relying on your new identity. Create a 6-segment Erased Past timer; when it fills, one intimate from your old life senses the deception and may investigate.
rites.push_it: Extend the metamorphosis to a willing ally, make the change permanent (lose access to one Bond or Minor Asset), or arrange a plausible 'death' for your old self (a funeral, a witness). Mark +2 Obligation and the GM gains 2 SB (the world strains to remember what was lost). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +3) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

cantors.name: The Cantor's Song
cantors.description: A Cantor of Isoka sings in whispers of shedding — melodies that rise and fall like a serpent's undulation, with harmonies that slither rather than resolve. Their voice is used to ease a difficult transformation (ritual scarring, a change of identity, the acceptance of loss) or to accelerate a foe's destructive change (madness, mutation, despair). Isoka's Cantors are often found in snake cults, their songs weaving venom and mercy in equal measure.

cult.name: The Cult of the Coiled Heart
cult.description: Isoka's cults are secretive, dangerous, and obsessed with metamorphosis. They gather in sunken temples, caverns beneath city sewers, or groves where adders nest. A ritual of the Coiled Heart involves each member holding a live serpent while speaking a name they wish to shed: a debt, a crime, a former allegiance. The serpent is then released into a central pit. Then they drink a tea brewed from shed snake skin and a drop of venom — the tea induces vivid dreams of their old self dying and a new self emerging. The most devoted replace one of their teeth with a hollow fang, allowing them to deliver a venomous bite (once per session, treat as a light melee weapon with the [POISON] tag). Their creed is carved in ouroboros rings: 'What devours itself is never consumed by another.' Outsiders are rarely invited; those who stumble into a rite are offered a choice — join, drink venom and be remade, or be forgotten as the cult sheds their memory.

witchcraft.name: The Art of the Scale and Venom
witchcraft.description: A witch who walks with Isoka is a scale-smith or venomer — one who understands that transformation is a craft. Their magic works with the materials of change: a forge that tempers steel by 'shedding' impurities, an alembic that distills venom into medicine, or a loom that weaves a new identity from discarded threads. Unlike the darker cults, these witches focus on healing and gentle release — helping a grief-stricken parent shed their sorrow, or a recovering addict shed their craving. Their tools are delicate: obsidian blades, silver alembics, and bundles of shed snakeskin. Isoka's witches craft poisons, but also transformation potions and magical clothing to alter appearance — they understand that the truest magic is not in changing the world, but in changing the self.
witchcraft.lore: The scale-smith's path is the art of transformation. They learn that every self is temporary, every identity a skin to be shed, and every ending a beginning. Isoka teaches that the venom that burns is the same that heals, and that the knife that cuts away the old self is the same that carves the new. These witches are found in quiet workshops, tending alembics and looms, their hands stained with venom and their eyes always searching for the next change.
witchcraft.quote: Do not mourn the skin you shed. It was never meant to last.

shedding_knife.name: The Shedding Knife
shedding_knife.description: A small, curved blade of obsidian or serpentine, never used for combat — only for cutting away what is no longer needed. Once per session, the witch may cut a physical token of an old identity (a lock of hair, a uniform patch, a letter) and burn it. For the remainder of the session, they gain +1 die on all rolls to deceive, hide, or escape detection, as the old self's traces are literally erased. The knife can also be used to 'shed' a minor curse or enchantment from a willing subject (remove one magical Condition with a touch, costing 1 Fatigue).

hedge_gifts.name: Venom's Mercy
hedge_gifts.description: Once per scene, the witch may apply a drop of harmless (or carefully dosed) venom to a wound, a drink, or a lock. Choose one effect: remove 1 Fatigue from an ally (as a mild stimulant), impose –1 die on a target's next physical roll (a mild paralytic), or force a target to speak a single truthful sentence (a truth serum). The victim may resist with a Resolve test (DV 3) if they are aware of the venom.

hedge_gifts.name: Shedding Skin
hedge_gifts.description: You may shed a minor physical tell — a scar, a birthmark, a distinctive tattoo — as if it were a snake shedding its skin. The tell regrows in a week unless you maintain the shedding. Once per session.

hedge_gifts.name: Venomous Alchemy
hedge_gifts.description: You may brew a single dose of a transformative potion during downtime. Choose one: a healing tincture (clears 1 Fatigue), a truth serum (target must test Resolve DV 3 to lie), or a mild poison (imposes –1 die on a target's next physical action). Requires an alembic and one scene of work.

hedge_gifts.name: Serpent's Grace
hedge_gifts.description: You gain +1 die to Athletics rolls involving climbing, squeezing, or balancing. Additionally, you may squeeze through gaps that would normally be too narrow for your frame. Passive.

monastic_tradition.name: The Way of the Coiled Serpent
monastic_tradition.description: Monks of the Coiled Serpent embody Isoka's philosophy of transformation. They move with the fluidity of a snake, strike with the precision of a viper, and shed their old selves as easily as a serpent sheds its skin. They understand that the greatest strength is not in holding on, but in letting go — of debts, of identities, of attachments that no longer serve. In the quiet of the monastery, they practice the art of shedding, learning that every ending is a beginning, and that the venom that burns away the old self is the same that grants the strength to become new.
monastic_tradition.prerequisites: Spirit 3+, Body 2+, Rite of the Loosening Skin or Cantor of Isoka.
monastic_tradition.quote: Do not mourn the skin you shed. It was never meant to last.
monastic_tradition.debt_resistant_frame: Serpents shed obligation as they shed skin. Monks of the Coiled Serpent gain +1 die to ignore or break a magical debt, geas, or contract (once per scene). When they do, a phantom snakeskin sloughs off them — the creditor may find an empty husk instead of a debtor.

basic.name: Venom Strike
basic.description: Unarmed hit can inject poison: choose –1 die to target's physical actions, or the target must speak a single truthful sentence (Resolve DV 3 to resist).

advanced.name: Hypnotic Sway
advanced.description: Once per scene, roll Presence + Lore vs. Resolve (DV 3) to mesmerize a single target. Your serpentine gaze holds them in thrall.

master.name: Ascendant Serpent
master.description: Once per session, gain a partial serpent-body: immune to mundane poison, +2 dice to Body rolls, and you may 'shed' one active debt or obligation entirely (the paperwork turns to dust). After the scene, you gain a permanent Debt Scar — a subtle pattern of scales on your arm — but you also gain +1 die on all rolls to resist future debts (the Hollow is less interested in those who have already shed so much).

monastic_tradition.corruption_note: Monks follow the patron's general Corruption track; the monastic path does not add a second one. Where a tradition needs its own, it must differ from the general track in kind, not degree.

corruption.benefit: Serpent's Gaze: +1 die on Intimidation or social rolls using menace.
corruption.cost: Cold-Blooded: –1 die on Empathy or warmth-based Persuasion.

corruption.benefit: Shed the Old Skin: Once/session, negate one Condition (Fear, Fatigue, Poison) by discarding it like molted skin.
corruption.cost: Mark of Scales: Faint reptilian patches visible, causing +1 SB in social encounters if noticed.

corruption.benefit: Venomous Strike: Bite or kiss may inflict Poison (DV 2).
corruption.cost: Hungry Coil: Must consume raw meat or eggs weekly, or mark 1 Fatigue.

corruption.benefit: Serpentine Grace: +2 dice to Stealth or Evasion rolls, ignore minor movement penalties.
corruption.cost: Slitted Eyes: Bright light imposes –1 die on Notice rolls.

corruption.benefit: Hypnotic Sway: Once/scene, roll Presence + Lore vs. Resolve (DV 3) to mesmerize a single target.
corruption.cost: Forked Tongue: –1 die on Deception when attempting warmth or sincerity.

corruption.benefit: Ascendant Form: Partial serpent-body; immune to mundane poison, +2 dice on Body rolls.
corruption.cost: Monstrous Aspect: Cannot easily hide your nature; every session begins with 1 SB that may be compelled by the GM.

playstyle_notes.description: Isoka's gifts make transformation useful before they make it frightening. A healer may shed grief; an infiltrator may discard a face that people loved. Keep track of what survives each change and who still recognizes the follower. The Coiled Heart's forced transformations are the cult's practice, not proof that everyone who accepts Isoka's help has consented to the same end.
emphasizes: Serpentine Transformation: shedding old selves, growing new ones
Venom as Dual Force: healing or destroying, depending on intent
Healthy Change vs. Sword-and-Sorcery Cults: from gentle alchemy to monstrous rebirth
Erasure of the Past: forgetting debts, identities, and old allegiances
Obsidian and Scale: the witch's craft of delicate shedding vs. the cult's venomous bite

sample_adventure.title: The Coiled Heart's Venom
sample_adventure.description: A member of the Coiled Heart cult has been found dead, their body covered in serpentine markings that were not there before. The cult believes they were trying to shed their humanity — and failed. Now the markings are spreading to others who were present at the ritual. The party must investigate the cult, discover the source of the markings, and decide whether to help the survivors complete their transformation, or to sever their connection to Isoka before the serpent claims them all. But some of the marked do not want to be saved — they have tasted the venom of change, and they hunger for more.
sample_adventure.quote: The serpent does not ask permission to shed. It simply grows until the skin splits, and then it leaves the old behind. Some transformations are chosen. Others are endured. And some — the most dangerous — are desired.

guises.name: The Copperhead
guises.note: A miniature portrait may be repainted while its frame remains in the same place. Copperhead keepers teach entrants to recognize the household's daily habits before changing their own appearance. Some return with the sought information and a tenderness for people they were hired to deceive. Others retain the borrowed manners after forgetting whom the manners once pleased.

guises.name: The Tide-Shedder
guises.note: A petitioner leaves hair and a name at a landing where eels enter the shrine. Returning boats carry people who recognize the route more readily than the names shouted from the quay. Households have developed quiet ways of receiving them without demanding an immediate account. Those customs can offer shelter and conceal how much has been lost.

guises.name: The Scale-Mother
guises.note: A cast skin is left undisturbed beside the threshold until its keeper removes it. Visitors do not bring one as a substitute offering. The household continues tending the person inside even when the name by which they ask for water changes. Nobody at the meal offers an explanation of what has grown too tight.

guises.name: The Sister of the Loosened Coil
guises.note: Traveling venomers brought Isoka's sign to places already honoring protective water serpents. Some workshops depict an empty skin beside a sheltering hood; their neighbors insist the two belong to different powers. A restored shrine may house both images without settling the identification. The person seeking bodily change can receive a different welcome from the family asking protection for its boat.

provenance.origin: Isoka belongs to the established triad with Ikasha and Inaea. The surviving histories concern how communities learned to approach her, not a replacement genealogy.
provenance.summary: Early accounts kept by the Coiled Heart have often been copied under names their keepers later abandoned. A text can preserve a chain of instruction while leaving uncertain whether successive signatures identify different teachers. Acasian copies dwell on faces and access; Zakov's versions preserve departures. Valewood households keep acts whose explanation would be unwelcome even when the action is taught carefully.
provenance.the_migration: Practices traveled through practitioners who needed somewhere to work after leaving an earlier life. Instruments, illustrated cloths, and portable household images crossed with them. In Ayokha, local serpent observances gave visitors a vocabulary for discussing protection and change. The resulting workshops never agreed that a common image established a common Patron. Some returned west with river titles and were accused of introducing a cult their teachers had already helped carry east.
provenance.why_it_took: Isoka's help can be real before it becomes frightening. A person may be able to return to work, bear an old loss, or escape an identity enforced by others. The Coiled Heart's inner discipline becomes coercive when it treats every hesitation as another shell to break. Quiet practitioners sometimes shelter people who refuse the next transformation. They may find that the sheltered person still longs for it.
provenance.note: A chosen change of life or identity is not itself evidence of corruption. The terror concerns supernatural losses and compulsory transformations: who still recognizes a familiar kindness, what cannot be recovered, and whether the transformed person is allowed to stop. These traditions do not place serpents in Theona.

philosophy.name: Who May Decide What Is Shed
philosophy.summary: Something that once protected a person can become restrictive. It does not follow that everything remembered deserves removal.
philosophy.the_point: A keeper may become proud of knowing what another person must outgrow. Refusal then becomes evidence of the keeper's diagnosis, and every result of the next transformation proves that it was necessary.
philosophy.the_third_thing: Some workshops preserve a small chosen object after a transformation without requiring its owner to explain why. Others destroy every such object as unfinished work. A preserved cup can become unbearable to someone who remembers its weight but nothing of the hand that gave it.
philosophy.at_the_table: Ask what the character seeks to change and what they value retaining. Show specific effects rather than declaring an ordinary identity monstrous. Keep coercive cult practices distinct from voluntary aid, and allow the person affected a say in the next intervention.
